title: A machine-learned dynamical phase diagram of the one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger equation with quasiperiodic disorder and a static field
abstract: We map the transport regimes of a wave packet evolving under the one-dimensional discrete nonlinear Schrödinger (Gross-Pitaevskii) equation with a quasiperiodic Aubry-André potential and a static (Stark) field, as a function of self-interaction $g$, field $F$, and quasiperiodic strength $λ$, for two initial states (delta and Gaussian). Instead of one expensive long-time simulation per grid point, we run 3600 short simulations, reduce each to eight dynamical features, and cluster parameter space with a Gaussian mixture model. Clustering finds the boundaries between regimes unsupervised; each cluster's name is then assigned by a hand-calibrated rule, and an ablation shows clustering measurably smooths those boundaries rather than merely relabeling them. The five resulting regimes (ballistic, localized, oscillatory-localized, subdiffusive, and self-trapped) are validated against 100 long runs on a lattice eight times larger than the short sweep, so the validation window is longer than the training window even for the fastest-spreading regime. The short-time clusters predict the long-time asymptotic spreading exponent ($α_\infty = 2.01\pm0.07$ ballistic, $0.28\pm0.16$ subdiffusive, consistent with the weak-chaos prediction $α=1/3$) and, independently, a long-time retention $Π_0=0.72\pm0.32$ for the self-trapped cluster, whose exponent alone is not diagnostic. The initial-state contrast is striking: the delta state develops a broad self-trapping wedge (onset at $g=3.907\pm0.017$ at $λ=0$) that invades the ballistic and localized regions as $g$ grows, while the Gaussian state shows no self-trapping, instead opening a subdiffusive corridor along the Aubry-André critical line that widens with $g$. The scheme yields a full $15\times15$ phase map in minutes per slice, where direct asymptotic simulation ($t\gtrsim10^6$ per point) is prohibitive.
summary: This work maps the dynamical phase diagram of a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with quasiperiodic disorder using machine learning to overcome the computational bottleneck of long-time simulations. By clustering features from short runs, the authors identify five distinct transport regimes, demonstrating that the initial state significantly alters the resulting dynamics. This provides a powerful, efficient tool for characterizing complex quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The paper aims to map the complex dynamical phase diagram of a nonlinear wave equation subjected to both quasiperiodic disorder and a static field.
main_result: Five distinct dynamical regimes (ballistic, localized, subdiffusive, etc.) are identified, and the study highlights the crucial role of initial state (delta vs. Gaussian) in determining the long-time dynamics.
method: It employs a machine-learning approach using Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) on features extracted from numerous short-time simulations to rapidly partition the high-dimensional parameter space.
model_or_system: The system is governed by the one-dimensional discrete nonlinear Schrödinger (Gross-Pitaevskii) equation, incorporating a quasiperiodic Aubry-André potential and a static (Stark) field.
key_observables: Spreading exponent ($\alpha_\infty$), long-time residual peak norm ($\Pi_0$), second moment ($m_2$), and various cluster-derived dynamical features.
important_parameters: Self-interaction strength ($g$), static field ($F$), and quasiperiodic strength ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: The physical regimes are assigned labels based on hand-calibrated rules applied to the unsupervised clustering results, and the method relies on short-time simulations predicting long-time asymptotics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate space-time density portraits and corresponding $m_2(t)$ curves for representative dynamics across the identified regimes, validating the short-time predictions against long-time behavior.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical model and the computational challenge, details the ML-assisted feature extraction and clustering methodology, presents the resulting phase maps for different initial states, and validates the identified regimes against long-time simulations.
why_interesting: The combination of nonlinear wave dynamics, quasiperiodic disorder (a hallmark of localization studies), and the use of ML for phase diagram construction is highly relevant to modern research in non-equilibrium quantum dynamics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Figure 2: Machine-learned dynamical phase diagrams. Rows: slices A (F = 0, g vs. λ) and B (λ = 1, g vs. F). Columns: delta and Gaussian initial states. White dots mark crossover cells, where the per-point threshold rule disagrees with its cluster’s majority-vote name (Sec. 4.4).

Figure 3: Validation against long-time ground truth. Left: asymptotic exponent α∞by short-time cluster (dashed lines mark the weak- and strong-chaos values 1/3 and 1/2; tv annotations give the median achieved tvalid per phase). Center: long-time (log10 m2, α∞) colored by short-time phase. Right: long-time residual peak norm Π0 by short-time cluster, the direct self-trapping check that does not rely on α∞.
Figure 4: PCA of the standardized short-time feature matrix, by initial state (rows), with cluster identity colored (left) and PCA loadings (right).

Figure 4 shows the first two principal components of the standardized feature matrix, which together capture most of its variance (66%+19% delta, 80%+12% gaussian). PC1 is dominated by the delocalization block (αm2, log m2, log P, growth) and PC2 by the retention/oscillation block (peak- drop, Bloch score, center-of-mass). The two physically independent axes, “how far/fast” and “what stayed behind”, emerge from the clustering without being hand-specified, even though the cluster names are (Sec. 4.4). The self-trapped cluster in the delta panel visibly splits into two PC1- separated clouds, the geometric signature of the α∞bimodality quantified in Sec. 5.3.
